title: Vayetze: a tenth (Genesis 28:20–22)
hook: Jacob vows a tenth of all he is given, a root of Jewish giving

segments.voice: Yesterday, a ladder in a plain place, and Jacob waking up. Your line was and I knew it not. This morning, Jacob makes a promise.

Look at your last paycheck, or your last grocery receipt, or the hours in your week. Somewhere in there is the question every budget asks: what's mine, and what do I give away? Jacob, the morning after his dream, owns almost nothing: a staff, the clothes he slept in, and the stone that was his pillow. He sets that stone up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and makes a vow. The vow is about money he doesn't have yet.
screen: `WHAT'S MINE, WHAT DO I GIVE?` → `A STAFF AND A STONE.` → `A VOW ABOUT MONEY HE DOESN'T HAVE.`

segments.voice: Jacob's vow is a list of plain needs. If God will be with me, and keep me on this road, and give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and I come back to my father's house in peace, then this stone will be God's house. Then the last line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and of all that Thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto Thee." In Hebrew it's doubled: aser a'asrenu, I will tenth it, a tenth. A promise said twice, for emphasis. Notice where he starts: not from surplus, from zero. He's promising a tenth of whatever he'll someday have, before he has any of it. He isn't the first. His grandfather Abraham gave a tenth of the spoils of war to Melchizedek, a priest-king. Later, the Torah turns the tenth into law: a tithe of the harvest, shared with the Levite, the stranger, the orphan and the widow. The word for tithe is ma'aser, from the Hebrew for ten, and later Jewish custom also speaks of ma'aser kesafim, a tenth of money. Maimonides, the great medieval teacher, wrote that giving a fifth of what you have is the finest way, a tenth is the ordinary way, and less than that is a stingy eye. The Talmud makes a gentle pun, too. Aser, to tithe, sounds like osher, wealth: give a tenth so that you'll become rich. The same passage even calls this the one place where testing God is allowed, citing the prophet Malachi. Either way, the pun ties giving and wealth together in one sound.
screen: `IF GOD WILL BE WITH ME…` · `ASER A'ASRENU: A TENTH, TWICE.` · `ABRAHAM, THEN THE HARVEST, THEN MONEY.` · `A FIFTH, A TENTH, A STINGY EYE.` · then, large: `I WILL SURELY GIVE THE TENTH.`

segments.voice: Choose something to set a tenth of aside; it doesn't have to be money. A tenth of your day is about two and a half hours, a tenth of an hour is six minutes, or a tenth of your pantry or this week's paycheck. Picture setting that tenth apart for someone who needs it more than you do, and notice how it feels to decide before you spend.
Ma'aser. A tenth, a tithe: what Jacob vowed with nothing in his pocket, and a root of Jewish giving ever since.
Your line: give a tenth. Jacob promised it before he had a thing. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jews give ma'aser kesafim, a tenth of their income, to tzedakah, often keeping a running account of what they owe to it; the biblical tithes of produce are still set aside in a symbolic way in Israel.
